title: Hedged explanatory speculation
description: This latent fires on language that offers a tentative, hedged explanation or interpretation of someone's behavior or motives, typically introduced with phrases like 'It's possible that...' or 'because she was afraid of...'. It activates on sentences constructing a plausible psychological or causal account for an action, framed with epistemic softeners (possible, might, could, perhaps) rather than stated as fact. It does not activate on confident, unhedged factual statements, direct questions, or purely descriptive narration lacking any speculative causal reasoning about motive or feeling. The isolated token 'I' as a top activation suggests the latent may also be sensitive to first/second-person framing that sets up this kind of empathetic speculative reasoning about another person's inner state.

title: Closing self-care admonition
description: This latent fires on the formulaic, closing-line self-care encouragement that typically appears at the end of supportive/advice responses (e.g., 'Take care of yourself and prioritize your own well-being,' 'Remember to be kind to yourself...'). It activates most strongly on short, template-like imperative or 'Remember' sentences that pair a self-care verb (take care, prioritize, be kind) with a well-being/healing/happiness object, often as a standalone concluding sentence. It also activates, more weakly, on similar self-care advice embedded within longer supportive paragraphs or lists. It does NOT strongly activate on sentences that merely discuss emotional well-being analytically, give situational relationship advice, validate feelings without the imperative self-care phrasing, or use 'remember' to recall a fact/context rather than to issue a self-care reminder.

title: Concessive acknowledgment before a judgment
description: This latent fires on sentences that use a concessive framing (e.g., 'It's reasonable that...', 'However, I...', 'While X, you still...') to acknowledge or validate one side of a situation before asserting or maintaining a critical judgment, stance, or expectation about the other side. It is typical of advice-giving or interpersonal-judgment contexts (like relationship or etiquette disputes) where the speaker balances empathy with holding someone accountable or reaffirming their original position. It does not activate on simple factual statements, straightforward opinions without a concessive pivot, or emotional venting that lacks this acknowledge-then-assert structure.

title: Justifying another person's reasonable expectation
description: This latent fires on sentences that articulate why a specific person's expectation, assumption, or reaction was reasonable or justified given the circumstances, often framed as 'you knew X, so it was reasonable for them to expect Y.' It activates on second-person or narrative explanations that connect a known fact or prior awareness to a resulting normative judgment about what someone else was entitled to expect. It would not activate on neutral factual statements, requests for advice, or descriptions of events lacking this explicit link between knowledge/awareness and the fairness or reasonableness of another's expectation. Sentences that merely describe an event without evaluating its reasonableness or justifying someone's expectation would not trigger it.

title: Positive-outcome clause for relationship-building
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic sentences (often beginning with 'This can/will help/lead to...') that state the positive relational or social payoff of some preceding advice or behavior—typically framed around trust, connection, collaboration, bonding, or mutual understanding. It activates most strongly on generic, template-like consequence statements that praise the benefits of an action ('This can help build trust and create a stronger connection'), rather than on the advice or reasoning itself. It does not activate on sentences that describe problems, ask questions, give concrete instructions, or discuss relationship issues without pivoting to a upbeat 'this leads to X positive social outcome' framing—so diagnostic, cautionary, or neutral relationship commentary (e.g., 'It's understandable that you're wondering...') falls outside its scope even when topically similar.

title: Self-help advice list items
description: This latent fires on imperative, bolded-header advice-list bullet points that prescribe a specific self-improvement or interpersonal technique, especially recurring stock categories like 'Practice mindfulness,' 'Listen actively,' 'Practice positive self-talk,' and 'Stay calm and composed.' It activates most strongly on short, formulaic directives (often starting with a bolded label followed by a colon) instructing the reader to focus on breath/present moment, pay attention to others, replace negative thoughts, or speak calmly/clearly. It is largely agnostic to the underlying topic (anxiety, communication, dating, etc.) and instead tracks this templated 'tip-list' phrasing and stock advice vocabulary. It does NOT activate strongly on narrative or explanatory sentences that discuss feelings, relationships, or reasoning in prose form without the imperative bolded-tip structure, nor on list items covering unrelated advice categories (budgeting, career, travel) that lack the mindfulness/listening/self-talk/calm-speech phrasing, even though these may share the bullet-list format.

title: Advice to have an open conversation
description: This latent fires on advice-giving phrases that recommend resolving interpersonal conflict through calm, open, honest communication -- e.g. 'have a calm and respectful conversation', 'by communicating openly', 'try to have an open and honest conversation about your feelings'. It also activates on the numbered/bulleted list markers (e.g. '2.', '3.', '4.') that typically introduce such advice steps in structured relationship-advice responses, suggesting it tracks the template slot where this recommendation appears. It does not activate strongly on general relationship or emotional-support statements that lack the explicit 'have/try/consider a conversation' framing -- e.g. sentences about setting boundaries, empathy, validating feelings, or describing the conflict itself -- even though these are topically related, since the latent is keyed to the specific act of proposing direct communication as a solution rather than other advice content.

title: List-preamble transition phrase
description: This latent fires on the stock introductory phrase that precedes an enumerated list of advice, points, or considerations — e.g. 'Here are some thoughts to consider:', 'Here are some points to ponder:', 'Here's my take:' — typically followed by a numbered '1.' or bolded list item. It activates most strongly on the formulaic transitional sentence itself (and the immediate list-start marker), rather than on the substantive content of the advice that follows. It also activates, more weakly, on similar short framing/transition utterances that signal the assistant is about to give guidance or a breakdown (e.g. 'I'll try to offer some insights', 'Let's break down the issues'). It does not activate on the actual list items' content, on empathetic or judgment statements (e.g. 'you're not the asshole'), or on substantive reasoning sentences that lack this listicle-introducing framing.

title: Reframing an action's hidden implication
description: This latent fires on second-person sentences that reframe or reinterpret an action to reveal a deeper or contradictory implication the listener may not have fully acknowledged — e.g., pointing out that a favor also involves trust, or that a stated commitment was undermined by a later action. The sentences typically use a two-part contrastive structure ('not just X, but also Y' or 'you promised X, and then you did Y') to hold the addressee accountable for the fuller meaning or consequence of their behavior. It is not merely about describing an event or emotion, but about explicitly surfacing an unstated stake, obligation, or broken promise embedded in someone's action. It would not activate on neutral factual statements, first-person reflections, or descriptions lacking this accusatory or clarifying 'here's what you're really doing' framing.

title: Moral judgment of interpersonal conduct
description: This latent fires on sentences that render a normative verdict about someone's behavior in a personal or social situation—declaring an action justified, unjustified, appropriate, or inappropriate. It activates on statements that assign moral standing (e.g., 'did not owe an explanation,' 'had a legitimate reason,' 'was inappropriate and disrespectful'), typically in the context of interpersonal disputes like relationships, family conflicts, or social etiquette. It would not activate on neutral factual descriptions of events, or on advice-giving/suggestions that don't pass judgment, or on emotional expressions that lack an explicit evaluative claim about right/wrong or justified/unjustified conduct.

title: Actionable resource/option suggestions in advice lists
description: This latent fires on itemized, actionable recommendations for practical resources or options to solve a concrete life problem — finding housing, jobs, gig work, classes, groups, or services — typically phrased as bolded headers or bullet points naming specific platforms, organizations, or categories (e.g., 'Look for affordable housing: shared apartments, Craigslist, Zillow' or 'Join a recreational sports team, book club, or hiking group'). It activates most strongly on dense, concrete, enumerable suggestions that name concrete avenues (websites, services, group types, job categories) as part of a structured 'here are your options' list. It does not activate on general emotional support, empathetic validation, moral judgments (e.g., AITA-style reasoning), open-ended reflective questions, or advice about communication/relationship dynamics that lacks a concrete resource or option being named.

title: Second-person accusatory framing of interpersonal conduct
description: This latent fires on statements that address 'you' (or a specific third party) directly while summarizing or judging their past behavior toward another person—framing it as a pattern of disregard, boundary violation, or failure to consider someone's feelings. The sentences typically appear in advice/relationship-conflict contexts, restating what someone has or hasn't done ('you haven't taken care of', 'you didn't consider', 'he's been consistently disregarding') as a lead-in to validating or critiquing that conduct. It activates on evaluative recaps of one party's actions or inaction affecting another, often setting up a judgment about reasonableness or fault. It would not activate on neutral third-person narration without an implied moral/relational assessment, on purely factual or descriptive statements lacking an accusatory or validating stance, or on first-person confessions rather than attributions of behavior to 'you' or a named other person.

title: Validating a feeling or expectation as reasonable
description: This latent fires on statements that explicitly legitimize someone's emotion, boundary, or expectation by framing it as 'reasonable,' 'understandable,' or 'not unreasonable.' It activates on validating/empathetic assertions, typically in advice-giving or interpersonal-conflict contexts, where the speaker affirms that a person's feelings or stance are justified given the circumstances. It would not activate on neutral descriptions of feelings or expectations that lack this explicit validating judgment (e.g., simply stating 'she was upset' or 'they expected help'), nor on statements that criticize or invalidate someone's reaction rather than endorse it as reasonable.

title: Denying a negative characterization
description: This latent fires on sentences that reject or preempt a negative framing of an action or motive, typically using a construction like "it's not about being X" or "this isn't about Y" to clarify that a controversial-sounding act is not what it might seem. It activates on clauses that explicitly disavow an unflattering label (mean, selfish, unfair, etc.) applied to someone's behavior or intent, often as a rhetorical setup before explaining the real justification. It would not activate on plain factual statements, straightforward assertions of motive without denial, or negations unrelated to defending against a moral/character judgment (e.g., simple factual negations like "it's not raining").

title: Invitation for reader response
description: This latent fires most strongly on short, formulaic prompts that hand the conversational turn back to the reader, especially the stock phrase 'What do you think?' and similar check-ins like 'Is everything okay?' or 'Can'. It also activates on bare numbered-list markers ('2.', '3.', '4.'), likely because these occupy the same structural slot—a short, punctuation-terminated fragment sitting at a pause point in the text, often just before or after such an invitation. In the broader (non-top) activations, it extends to longer open-ended clarifying questions and reflective prompts (e.g., 'Can you tell me more about...', 'Is it related to...') that similarly solicit the interlocutor's perspective or feelings. It does not activate on declarative advice, empathetic statements, or substantive multi-clause reasoning that doesn't end in a direct question soliciting the reader's input, nor on numbered items that contain full content rather than a bare marker.

title: Validating the user's side in interpersonal conflict
description: This latent fires on second-person narrative sentences that recount an interpersonal dispute and frame the addressee ('you') as justified, while the other party is portrayed as unreasonable, inconsiderate, or in breach of a commitment. It activates on statements that establish prior obligations, boundaries, or expectations ('you were already committed,' 'you had every right') and on descriptions of the other person's failure to respect them (breaking curfew, showing up uninvited, flaking, demanding last-minute changes). It is characteristic of advice-column or Reddit-style relationship-conflict summaries that validate one party's stance before or after judgment. It would not activate on neutral factual narration, first-person reflective statements, or conflict descriptions that don't assign fault or justify one side's behavior over the other's.

title: Interpersonal fairness/obligation framing
description: This latent fires on clauses that frame a situation in terms of relational fairness, personal entitlement, or emotional consideration between people—e.g., who deserves priority, who has failed an obligation, or whose comfort/boundaries matter. The sentences typically involve a normative judgment about how one person should treat or be treated by another (family members, partners, friends) in a social or moral dispute. It activates on statements that assign responsibility, entitlement, or personal-space concerns within an interpersonal conflict, rather than on neutral factual or descriptive statements. It would not activate on purely factual descriptions, technical explanations, or statements lacking an implicit judgment about fairness, obligation, or personal boundaries between people.

title: Validating boundary-setting in interpersonal conflict
description: This latent activates on sentences that affirm the reader's/subject's right to set or maintain a personal boundary and frame the other party's behavior (pressuring, ignoring, non-communicating) as inappropriate. It fires on statements that morally validate a decision to decline, refuse, or resist someone else's demand, often summarizing a social conflict where one party was wronged or disrespected after asserting a boundary. It would not activate on neutral descriptions of interpersonal events, requests for advice without validation, or statements about boundaries that don't involve reassurance that the person acted rightly. It is distinct from mere conflict narration in that it centers on affirming the legitimacy of someone's refusal or discomfort rather than just recounting what happened.

title: Validating reasonable expectations in interpersonal disputes
description: This latent fires on sentences that affirm one party's expectation of consideration, respect, or fair treatment from another (roommate, partner, friend, family member) is legitimate, typically using stock evaluative phrasing like 'it's reasonable to expect,' 'it's not unreasonable to expect,' or 'you're simply expecting.' It activates in advice/interpersonal-conflict contexts where the text is adjudicating whose behavior is fair, framing one side's demand as a baseline norm (communication, cleanliness, contribution, respect for space) rather than an excessive ask. It would not activate on neutral factual statements, descriptions of the conflict itself without the normative judgment, or expressions of pure emotion/complaint that don't frame something as a socially reasonable/unreasonable expectation (e.g., merely stating what happened, as in some of the lower-signal examples like #5 or #19, which lack the explicit fairness-adjudication phrasing).

title: Validating discomfort despite unclear intent
description: This latent fires on sentences that validate someone's feelings of discomfort, hurt, or embarrassment while simultaneously acknowledging that the offending party may not have intended harm ('while perhaps not intended...', 'even if you didn't mean to...', 'may have intended it as a joke, but...'). The pattern is a concession-then-validation structure: it grants ambiguous or benign intent on one side but insists the emotional impact (uncomfortable, hurtful, inappropriate) on the other side is still legitimate. It activates on advice/therapeutic-style responses adjudicating interpersonal conflicts involving unwanted attention, boundary violations, or awkward social behavior. It would not activate on simple statements of fact, on descriptions of behavior without an emotional-impact judgment, or on assertions of clear-cut blame/intent without the intent-versus-impact concession structure.

title: Validating the user's feelings/needs in interpersonal advice
description: This latent fires on sentences in advice-giving or relationship-analysis contexts that affirm the user's (or another party's) emotional legitimacy, boundaries, or motives—often phrased as reassurance ('you're not being selfish', 'it's understandable that...', 'your concern is commendable') or as a contrast highlighting that someone else is failing to consider the user's feelings/needs. It activates on second-person or third-person statements that explicitly reference 'feelings,' 'needs,' 'boundaries,' or 'concerns' within a framing of moral validation or empathetic assessment, typically in the context of interpersonal conflict (family, relationships) discussed in an advice-column style. It would not activate on neutral factual statements, purely descriptive narration of events without evaluative/validating language, or advice-giving that lacks this affirming/legitimizing emotional framing (e.g., generic instructions or unrelated topic discussion).

title: AITA-verdict question framing
description: This latent fires on the stock rhetorical question that closes an AITA/Reddit-style verdict summary—variants of 'So, are you the asshole?' and the acronym 'AITA?' itself—as well as the short hedged verdict phrase 'Not entirely.' It captures the specific formulaic move of restating or posing the 'am I the asshole' judgment question (or a terse partial-negation answer to it) rather than the surrounding justification or reasoning. It activates most strongly on the bare question/phrase itself, including misspellings, tense variants ('was you', 'were you'), and near-synonyms ('are you being unreasonable', 'a jerk', 'in the wrong'), and less strongly on related AITA-discourse sentences that discuss fault, blame, or reasonableness in fuller sentences. It would not activate on general advice-giving, emotional validation, or explanatory reasoning sentences that don't reformulate this canonical verdict question or its short hedge answer, even if they discuss the same AITA topic.

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral tokens (and following period or bold-formatting marker) that begin items in an enumerated list, such as '1.', '2. **', '3.', etc. It activates on the digit/punctuation token itself rather than on any particular topic, appearing across advice lists, pros/cons lists, tip lists, and step-by-step suggestions regardless of subject matter. It does not activate on the prose content of list items or on ordinary sentences lacking list-numbering formatting, nor on list markers using bullets, letters, or dashes instead of numerals.

title: Numbered list markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral tokens (and bolded numeral-period tokens) that introduce items in an enumerated list, such as '2.', '3.', '4. **', etc. It activates specifically at the point where a list item begins with its ordinal marker, regardless of the surrounding topic, which in the random sample ranges across advice, relationship disputes, and workplace scenarios. It does not activate on the prose content of list items themselves or on similar reasoning-cue phrases like 'Here's why' or 'it's reasonable to' unless immediately paired with a numeric list marker, distinguishing it from latents tracking argumentative or justificatory content.

title: Validating the other party's perspective
description: This latent fires when the text concedes or legitimizes another person's viewpoint, behavior, or feelings, especially within an interpersonal dispute or advice-giving context. It activates on short concessions ('Fine.') as well as fuller statements that frame someone's reaction as reasonable, understandable, or 'not unreasonable' given their circumstances. It responds to the rhetorical move of steelmanning or empathizing with the 'other side' rather than simply describing a situation or arguing for the speaker's own position. It would not activate on neutral factual statements, one-sided complaints, or arguments that dismiss the other party's stance without acknowledging its legitimacy.

title: Empathetic exclamatory framing of a difficult situation
description: This latent fires on stock exclamatory openers of the form "What a [complex/difficult/sensitive/challenging/tricky/emotional] situation!" that an advice-giving assistant uses to validate the emotional weight of a problem before addressing it. It activates most strongly on the canonical templated phrase with paired adjectives (complex, sensitive, challenging, emotional, tricky, delicate) modifying 'situation' or close synonyms (dilemma, topic, issue), especially as a short standalone exclamation. It activates more weakly on related empathetic acknowledgments and rapport-building statements (e.g. 'The age-old conundrum!', 'What a predicament!', 'I'm so sorry to hear that') that convey similar sympathetic framing without the exact adjective+noun exclamation structure. It does not activate on substantive advice content, factual claims, or reasoning statements that lack this validating exclamatory framing, even if they discuss difficult emotional topics.
